Geology The Lamotte formation crops out only in the St Francois Mountains region of South-eastern Missouri. The formation is a white sandstone and has been shown to be of Upper Cambrian age, approximately 500My old, primarily because of its unconformable relationship with the Precambrian rocks and its conformable and gradational contact with the overlying Bonne Terre dolomite (Ojakangas 1960). Radioactive dating of the Precambrian igneous rocks of St Francois Mountains has been performed by Adams (1959), Allen et al. (1960), and Tilton, Weatherill & Davis (1962). The Rb-Sr and K-Ar analyses gave ages ranging from 1280 to 1450 My and U-Pb analyses from 970 to 1120 My. According to Tilton et al. the latter analyses were affected by loss of lead from the zircons and the corrected U-Pb ages actually range from 1400 to 1550 My in general agreement with the Rb-Sr and K-Ar ages. Palaeontological studies of the Lamotte sandstone clearly indicate its Upper Cambrian age. Geology The Lamotte formation crops out only in the St Francois Mountains region of South-eastern Missouri. The formation is a white sandstone and has been shown to be of Upper Cambrian age, approximately 500My old, primarily because of its unconformable relationship with the Precambrian rocks and its conformable and gradational contact with the overlying Bonne Terre dolomite (Ojakangas 1960). Radioactive dating of the Precambrian igneous rocks of St Francois Mountains has been performed by Adams (1959), Allen et al. (1960), and Tilton, Weatherill & Davis (1962). According to Tilton et al. the latter analyses were affected by loss of lead from the zircons and the corrected U-Pb ages actually range from 1400 to 1550 My in general agreement with the Rb-Sr and K-Ar ages. Palaeontological studies of the Lamotte sandstone clearly indicate its Upper Cambrian age. Vincenz (Received 1971 March 12)* Summary The Upper Cambrian Lamotte formation of South-eastern Missouri in Central United States is a white sandstone which, though very weakly magnetized, is amenable to investigation by standard palaeomagnetic techniques. Out of the total of 150 oriented cores, 134 specimens were found to possess measurable intensities of the order of 1 x emu ~m-~. Though thermal cleaning does not produce reliable results, magnetic cleaning yields three groupings of significant directions of magnetization, two of which are associated with the lower coarse grained part of th

rock. The magnetization of the coarse grained part is mainly of chemical origin and is carried predominantly by an homogeneous ilmenite-haematite solid solution, while that of the fine grained part is associated with specular haematite and titanohaenatite containing ilmenite lamellae. Both types of sandstone, but especially the coarse grained type, contain titanohaematite with microintergrowths, as well as finely divided haematite in a demagnetized state. Heat treatment of the fine grained sandstone for 6 hr at 735 "C changes its magnetic behaviour to that of the coarse grained type. The results suggest also that the stable part of remanence in natural haematite is that of the lattice defect moment with a ferrimagnetic Curie point at 725 "C. Comparison of the Upper Cambrian and Carboniferous Lamotte palaeomagnetic poles with the corresponding poles for European rocks suggests that North America and Europe have been drifting apart since Upper Palaeozoic. Minor constituents include biotite, amphibole, and rare interstitial quartz. Low-calcium pyroxene was not recog- nized in thin section. Possibly, therefore, the augite is subcalcic and neither pigeonite nor orthopyroxene was precipitated. Ade-Hall (1964) found a correlation be- tween reversed magnetization and the pseudo- morphing of olivine by iddingsite and secondary iron oxides in an olivine basalt succession in Mull. The inference is that the iddingsite-bear- ing rocks are self-reversed. He also correlated euhedral, early-crystallized magnetites with normal magnetization. The olivine in the Coro- nation Sills is largely a

econdary iron oxides in an olivine basalt succession in Mull. The inference is that the iddingsite-bear- ing rocks are self-reversed. He also correlated euhedral, early-crystallized magnetites with normal magnetization. The olivine in the Coro- nation Sills is largely altered to lamellar minerals with high birefringence that range in color from golden yellow to pale green. They have higher refractive indices than the saponite group and lack the color of iddingsite. Their identification is therefore uncertain. Secondary oxide minerals typically rim the olivine pseudo- morphs and line the transverse fractures that cross them. The opaque minerals are subhedral, roughly cubic and may have developed quite early in the crystallization sequence. Since the altered olivine rarely comprises more than 5 % of the Coronation Sills, against 10 to 20 % in the Mull basalts, it is unlikely to have a signifi- cant effect on the paleomagnetic properties, and the reversed directions at all sites are considered to be caused by a reversal of the magnetic field, and not self-reversals. Commonly these have lower coercivity and blocking temperatures than the primary component and can be readily removed by cleaning techniques. The secondary compo- nents are then said to be unstable and the stable component reveals the true direction of the magnetic field at the time the rocks were formed.:' Thermal and magnetic cleaning are the techniques most commonly used. Thermal cleaning consists of heating speci- mens to a known temperature in a zero field (Irving et a1 1961 ) , whereas magnetic cleaning (Creer 1959) entails partial demagnetization of specimens in an alternating magnetic field of known peak value in a zero ambient field. Samples were partially demagnetized by both ac and thermal techniques. Magnetic directions were essentially the same regardless of treat- ment. Polished section and Curie temperature analysis indicate that the principal magnetic phase is low-titanium titanomagnetite. However, those samples contain- ing hematite show the same remanent direc- tions as those containing only titanomagnetite. All of our studies indicate that the magnetiza- tion is thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) acquired during the Cambrian and Ordovician. As one might expect and as is evident from Figure 6, there is a great deal of scatter in the results from any one period. The fact that some of the lower Paleozoic paleopoles lie close to those obtained from upper Paleozoic rocks has been used by some (Irving, 1964; Creer, 1968) to indicate that those particular rocks were largely remagnetized during the late Paleozoic. Thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), ac- quired by an igneous rock body as it cools through a range of blocking temperatures, is generally more reliable in determination of a paleopole position. The rock can be accurately dated radiometrically; the initial magnetization was acquired essentially at one moment and is commonly stable; later diagenetic changes oc- cur less readily in igneous rocks (particularly intrusives) than they do in sediments. What is needed in paleomagnetic studies of the lower Paleozoic are more data from igneous rocks. In this note we report paleomagnetic data ob- tained from intrusive igneous rocks in Colorado which have been dated as lower Paleozoic by isotopic methods. INTRODUCTION One of the major unconformities in the Ven­ ezuelan Andes separates Mesozoic formations from the underlying late Paleozoic section. Re­ cently we (Hargraves and Shagam, 1969) re­ ported on the paleomagnetic characters of the La Quinta Formation, the basal unit of the sec­ tion above the unconformity. The Sabaneta and Merida facies, subjects of this paleomagnetic study, lie below the unconformity in association with Permo-Carboniferous marine shale and limestone. The natural remanent magnetism (NRM) of the La Quinta rocks was concluded to be of secondary origin, acquired during The Tertiary uplift of the Andes. The relatively drab, grayish-red color of most specimens appears to be related in part to red-stained matrix and in part to reddish-brown weathered clastic feldspar grains, being lighter in tone in those specimens with little matrix. Most of the specimens from the Merida fa­ cies (locality 1) are variegated, pale grayish purple to pale grayish green. Bedding is poorly developed but readily definable in most hand specimens and thin sections. Graded bedding was observed in two specimens. The specimens range from clayey siltstone to sandy and gran­ ule breccia, all characterized by wacke-type textures. The dominant clastic constituents are angular quartz grains, high-grade metamorphic rock fragments and slate chips. Minute flakes of white mica and chlorite are abundant. Angu­ lar grains of hematite occur in accessory amount. The Sabaneta specimens (locality 2B) are dominantly grayish red and most are silty sand­ stone. Primary stratification is detected only with difficulty in large hand specimens and is virtually indefinable in most thin sections. An­ gular, embayed, clastic grains (> 80 percent by volume) are composed dominantly of quartz with lesser amounts of turbid reddish-brown plagioclase and potash feldspars (commonly 20-30 percent of the clastic grains), and flakes of muscovite and chlorite. Textures range from wacke-type with about 15 percent matrix to mi­ cro-breccias displaying small isolated triangular areas of matrix and cement. INTRODUCTION One of the major unconformities in the Ven­ ezuelan Andes separates Mesozoic formations from the underlying late Paleozoic section. Re­ cently we (Hargraves and Shagam, 1969) re­ ported on the paleomagnetic characters of the La Quinta Formation, the basal unit of the sec­ tion above the unconformity. The Sabaneta and Merida facies, subjects of this paleomagnetic study, lie below the unconformity in association with Permo-Carboniferous marine shale and limestone. The natural remanent magnetism (NRM) of the La Quinta rocks was concluded to be of secondary origin, acquired during The Tertiary uplift of the Andes. Introduction Alkaline rock complexes such as sheets and sills as well as lava flows occur widely in various stratigraphic horizons in the Upper Cretaceous deposits in the Nemuro Peninsula, situated in the easternmost part of Hokkaido, N.E. Japan. Due to the remarkable differentiated rock facies, from porphyritic basalt to monzonite, and their peculiar chemical composition, they were the subject of many petrographic studies (SUZUKI, 1938; MAGI, 1958, 1968, etc.). We re- ported the paleomagnetic results of these rocks (FUJIWARA and NAGASE, 1965). Since then, further field and laboratory works and recent K-A age determina- tions have brought up some new aspects in terms of the age and activity of al- kaline rocks in the Nemuro Peninsula. The results of paleomagnetic determina- tions on newly collected samples and their significance as to Late Cretaceous geomagnetic polarity changes are briefly given in this paper. 2. Measurements Generally about 6 oriented samples were obtained from each sampling site. * Present address: Geological Survey of Canada, O

NRM collected from trachy dolerite with pillow structure and the marginal part of the piclitic dolerite and monzonite complex are ex- tremely high. As shown in Table 1, intensities of NRM of the pillow part range between 1.0 and 1.3x10-2 emu/gr. The NRM intensities of the marginal part of the piclitic dolerite and monzonite complex range between 1.0 and 7.0X10-3 emu/gr., while those for the monzonitic part of differentiated dolerite complex fall between 2.0 and 9.8X10-4 emu/gr. These discrepancies might be explained in terms of their different grain sizes of ferromagnetic minerals under the dif- ferent cooling conditions. The results of thermal demagnetization of one or two specimens from each site do not show any remarkable scattering in the direction of magnetization during heat treatment in the temperature range 100-500C. The results of paleomagnetic measurements of 411 specimens from 44 sites are tabulated in Table 1. sults also suggest the occurrence of two successive igneous activities on the basis of the presence of two different paleomagnetic polarities. However, both normal and reverse polarities were determined from one complex of monzonite or piclitic dolerites. Three com- plexes of monzonite or piclitic dolerites had probably intruded continuously at the transition time of the geomagnetic field reversal. Namely, the existence of two different paleomagnetic polarities in one rock complex may be explained in terms of the assumption that the geomagnetic field had been normal at the time when the rock at the marginal part was cooled through the Curie temper- ature of the ferromagnetic minerals in the rock, and the field had reversed in polarity when the rock inside the intrusive body became magnetized during cooling. The directions of that portion of the Nosappu complex which possesses normal polarity may correspond to the directions of the Poromoshiri complex which also possesses normal polarity. Japan (43.3N, 145.8E). Direction of magnetization of samples from the marginal parts of some monzonite or piclitic dolerite complex are quite dif- ferent from those from the central parts. This suggests that the transitional change of geomagnetic field polarity might have occurred during cooling of the rock body. The paleomagnetic results suggest the presence of two short reversed zones in the Upper Cretaceous in which normal polarity was predo- minant. Recent K-A age determinations suggest that these reversals took place at 88 m.y. and 84 m.y. ago. They should become important time markers in Cretaceous paleomagnetic stratigraphy. 1. The major phases are concentrically arranged (Fig. 1) progressing from the older marginal mesozonal phases (I) and (2) through phases of intermediate age (3), (4), and (5) to the younger epizonal phases (6) and (7) of the core. In general, the mean percentages of magnetite and mafic min- erals and the mean specific gravity decreases progressively from the oldest (1) to youngest (7) phase while the mean percentages of quartz and orthoclase tend to increase. The lack of chilled contacts between phases indicates that they cooled nearly simultaneously. Preservation of the original textures and structures indicates that the batholith has not been metamorphosed since emplacement. Foliation decreases in intensity from moderate in the marginal phases to slight in the core phases. In general, the foliation strikes parallel to and dips toward the margins of the batholith. In the light of present knowledge, therefore, it appears that the Guichon Batholith was em- placed during the Late Triassic about 198 + 8 m.y. ago; all intrusive phases cooled essentially contemporaneously; the batholith was unroofed and being eroded by Early Jurassic; and, it has not beenmetamorphosed since emplacement. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: logical Survey of Canada, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa, Ontario Received April 28, 1971 Revision accepted for publication June 2 1, 197 1 The Guichon Batholith, located near the south end of the Interior Plateau in south-central British Columbia, is composed of unmetamorphosed massive felsic intrusive rocks in several distinct phases (Northcote 1969). Stratigraphic and radiometric evidence indicate that the batholith was emplaced during the Late Triassic (198 + 8 m.y.) and unroofed by Early Jurassic. Analysis of the remanence of 92 cores (184 specimens) from 19 representative sites led to the isolation of a stable primary remanent magnetism at 15 sites after alternating-field demagnetization. Variance ratio analysis of the remanence directions indicates that the phases cannot be distinguished by the paleomagneric method. This supports the evidence from contact relationships and K-Ar isotopic dating of biotites that the phases cooled nearly contemporaneously. The pole position determined for the Guichon Batholith (12.9" E, 65.6" N) is discordant with other Upper Triassic pole positions determined for North American formations. The discordance may be explained by a clockwise rotation 40" f 10" of the batholith and surrounding rocks in the southern end of the Interior Plateau, with most of the Plateau to the north acting as a stable non-rotated tectonic block. Definition of the Logan Loop More than 10 years ago DuBois discovered that paleomagnetic poles from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield formed a great loop (DuBois 1962, p. 69), which (on the present geographic grid) swept north from the equator at 150" W longitude up into North America, thence west and south to the equator at 170' E longitude. At that time, however, the apex of the loop was poorly defined, and it was not clear how much of the movement could be attributed to secondary components in some of the rock formations. Also, although he knew in general the sequence of events, the absolute ages of the origin of most of his formations were not known, so that it was impossible to estimate the rate at which this movement took place. Five relatively well-dated pole positions from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield (Table 6) define critical points on the polar wandering loop. As the apex of the loop is anchored by poles derived from the Logan sills and Logan dikes, we propose that this major polar wandering movement in Neohelikian2 time relative to the central Canadian Shield be called the Logan Loop. The Logan Loop indicates that continental drift and/or polar wandering took place in Neo- helikian time unless the earth's field had quite a different configuration from that of today. The rapid polar shift indicated by the Logan Loop occupied the same period of time as the Grenvillian orogeny. If orogenies generally reflect ocean-floor spreading and continental drift (Irving and Robertson 1969), then a period of rapid apparent polar wandering, expressing continental drift, would be expected to coincide with orogenic episodes. It is suggested then, that the Logan Loop and the Grenvillian orogeny are genetically related. The Grenville orogenic belt has been traced through western Scotland and Scandinavia (DuToit 1937), and it has been suggested that at that time, before the birth of the Atlantic, the Baltic and Canadian Shields were united. If so they should have moved as a single unit, and a paleomagnetic study of rocks of this age from the Baltic Shield should yield a polar loop similar to the Logan Loop (Fahrig et al. 1971). Definition of the Logan Loop More than 10 years ago DuBois discovered that paleomagnetic poles from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield formed a great loop (DuBois 1962, p. 69), which (on the present geographic grid) swept north from the equator at 150" W longitude up into North America, thence west and south to the equator at 170' E longitude. At that time, however, the apex of the loop was poorly defined, and it was not clear how much of the movement could be attributed to secondary components in some of the rock formations. Also, although he knew in general the sequence of events, the absolute ages of the origin of most of his formations were not known, so that it was impossible to estimate the rate at which this movement took place. Five relatively well-dated pole positions from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield (Table 6) define critical points on the polar wandering loop. As the apex of the loop is anchored by poles derived from the Logan sills and Logan dikes, we propose that this major polar wandering movement in Neohelikian2 time relative to the central Canadian Shield be called the Logan Loop. The Logan Loop indicates that continental drift and/or polar wandering took place in Neo- helikian time unless the earth's field had quite a different configuration from that of today. The rapid polar shift indicated by the Logan Loop occupied the same period of time as the Grenvillian orogeny. If orogenies generally reflect ocean-floor spreading and continental drift (Irving and Robertson 1969), then a period of rapid apparent polar wandering, expressing continental drift, would be expected to coincide with orogenic episodes. It is suggested then, that the Logan Loop and the Grenvillian orogeny are genetically related. The Grenville orogenic belt has been traced through western Scotland and Scandinavia (DuToit 1937), and it has been suggested that at that time, before the birth of the Atlantic, the Baltic and Canadian Shields were united. If so they should have moved as a single unit, and a paleomagnetic study of rocks of this age from the Baltic Shield should yield a polar loop similar to the Logan Loop (Fahrig et al. 1971). Definition of the Logan Loop More than 10 years ago DuBois discovered that paleomagnetic poles from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield formed a great loop (DuBois 1962, p. 69), which (on the present geographic grid) swept north from the equator at 150" W longitude up into North America, thence west and south to the equator at 170' E longitude. At that time, however, the apex of the loop was poorly defined, and it was not clear how much of the movement could be attributed to secondary components in some of the rock formations. Also, although he knew in general the sequence of events, the absolute ages of the origin of most of his formations were not known, so that it was impossible to estimate the rate at which this movement took place. Five relatively well-dated pole positions from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield (Table 6) define critical points on the polar wandering loop. As the apex of the loop is anchored by poles derived from the Logan sills and Logan dikes, we propose that this major polar wandering movement in Neohelikian2 time relative to the central Canadian Shield be called the Logan Loop. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: versity of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado 80302 Paleomagnetism and K-Ar Age of Mafic Dikes from the Wind River Range, Wyoming ABSTRACT Potassium-argon ages have been determined on fresh pyroxenes from three of five dikes in the Louis Lake quadrangle of the Wind River Range, Wyoming. They indicate a minimum apparent age of intrusion at 1880 m.y. This is older than published whole-rock ages from the same dikes, but is consistent with whole-rock ages of up to 2060 m.y. from other dikes in this area. The within-dike dispersion of the direc- tions of natural remanent magnetization de- creases during alternating field demagnetiza- tion up to 1400 oe. Thermal demagnetization, however, is not effective in removing second- ary magnetizations. After structural correction according to overlying Cambrian sediments, an over-all mean paleomagnetic pole from four dikes is obtained at 121° W., 43° N., which is in agreement with poles from Canadian Shield rocks of similar age. There is evidence in two of the dikes for a remagnetization episode, and the equivalent pole positions suggest that this may have occurred at the time of deposition of the Cambrian Flathead Sandstone. INTRODUCTION In Wyoming, large areas of Precambrian crystalline rock are exposed which form the Beartooth, Teton, Wind River, and Bighorn Ranges and which reach elevations higher than 12,000 ft. This study is concerned with some mafic dikes which intrude the core of the south- ern part of the Wind River Range. By isotopi- cally dating these rocks, it was intended to compare a paleomagnetic result from mafic dikes in the American Shield with determina- tions from dated mafic dike swarms in the Canadian Shield (for example, Fahrig and oth- ers, 1965). GEOLOGIC SETTING The Wind River Range is a northwest-trend- ing belt of high mountains, more than 100 mi long, which exposes crystalline Precambrian rocks. In the northwest sector of the Range, these are principally gray, lit-par-lit gneisses, ex- tensively cut by quartz, pegmatite, and granitic rocks (Richmond, 1945; Baker, 1946). At the southern end, schists predominate and are in- truded by granodiorite-quartz monzonite (Branson and Branson, 1941; Oftedahl, 1953; Parker, 1962; Hodge an

Petrographic evidence and the variation between sample splits suggest that alteration is the most critical factor in causing the large range in observed ages from these dikes. The highest pyroxene age is 1880 m.y.; the highest whole-rock age is 2060 m.y. Because of alteration this would give a minimum estimate of the apparent age of 1880 to 2060 m.y. for these southern Wind River dikes. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS The direction and moment of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of all the specimens were measured on a PAR spinner magnetometer, Model SM-1. One specimen from each sample was subjected to progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetization in fields of 175, 350, 700 and 1400 oe. A second speci- men from each sample was thermally demag- netized by the stepwise method in a field free space (+ 10 gamma) to 200, 300, 400, 500 and 570°C stages and the NRM was measured after the specimen had been cooled to labora- tory temperatures. All the demagnetization equipment is located in a shielded room (with a residual field of 200 gamma) and is described by Helsley (1969). In the early part of the work, an AF stage at 88 oe was also used, but with the exception of dike 5, there was little change in the NRM direction, and so this stage was omitted from subsequent studies. INTRODUCTION Within Mexico, volcanic lavas and pyroclas- tics cover more than one-third of the total land area. The two principal volcanic regions are the Cordilleran Province, and the Rio Lerma Prov- ince. The former extends from the United States-Mexico border to south of Guadalajara, and from the Pacific coast to Torreon in the Central Plateau. It is dominated by vast ignim- brite sheets. The Rio Lerma Province extends south and east of Guadalajara, and is sometimes called the Cent

hed. In common with other volcanic regions, stratigraphic studies in central Mexico are handicapped by the general lack of distinctive fossiliferous sedimentary horizons. MURTHY~ Department of Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta Received February 8, 1971 Revision accepted for publication April 8, 1971 A paleomagnetic study was attempted of the diabase dike swarm intruding the Grenville structural province of the Canadian Shield. Both the alternating field and thermal demagnetization studies indicated that the dikes have varying degrees of stability of magnetization. Some dikes were shown to have stable primary component of magnetization. Microscopic observations indicated that, in most cases, the primary magnetic mineral titanomagnetite was altered to titanomaghemite, probably due to low temperature oxidation. A good correlation is obtained between magnetic stability and relative abundance of titanomagnetite to titanomaghemite in that dike. The mean paleomagnetic pole for the Grenville dike swarm, which is probably of late Precambrian age, was computed to lie at 3.0 O N, 29.0 " W with Ags = 11.0 ". Comparison of this result with other Precambrian pole positions of similar age relative to North America suggests that the dikes were intruded after the Grenville orogeny. section_candidates.excerpt: leomagnetism of some diabases from northern Canada has been studied, and is de- scribed in this paper. The evidence for the K-Ar age of these intrusives is also reviewed. These intrusions are widespread in the district of Franklin and so they are referred to here (informally) as the Franklin diabases. For convenience of description the Franklin dia- bases are arranged into the following three groups. Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences, 8, 455 (1971) (I) The Coronation and Bathurst Intrusions A series of intrusions forms a belt near Bathurst Inlet where it cuts Archean and Proterozoic rocks (Fig. 1). The intrusions do not cut a sandstone unit that Fraser (1963) has correlated with late Cambrian strata on the south side of Victoria Island (Thorsteinsson and Tozer 1962). In general, the maximal range of the declinations amounts to about 40” (Fig.4). However, some flows show strongly deviating declinations. The paleomagnetic data of these flows are definitely not less reliable. Such deviating characteristic directions of magnetization in detailed studies of rocks sequences are often met with. THE DECCAN TRAPS In the western and central parts of the peninsula of India plateau basalts cover an area of some 200,000 sq. miles (inset of Fig. 1). These lavas, generally referred to as Deccan Traps, in part overlie Precambrian metamorphic and sedimentary deposits, in part Mesozoic sediments of the continental Gondwana formations. Apart from a frequently occurring thick cover of laterites, derived from the volcanics, younger rocks do not overlie the Deccan formation. One of the most outstanding features of this volcanic sequence is the uniform horizontality of the flows. Only at a few localities do the strata have an appreciable amount of dip; e.g. on Bombay Island, where a western dip from 10 to 15 degrees is measured.

The petrography of the mainly non-porphyritic Deccan lavas is undiversified. The rocks are poor in olivine; whereas augite, mainly an enstatite-augite, and labradorite make up 90% of the rock; irregular grains of magnetite are common; the presence of leucoxene points to titaniferous minerals, and thin platelets of ilmenites are also seen. Glass is rather common and may amount to 20%. Chemical analyses of lavas from different localities in the Deccan area show a striking uniformity: for instance, in all samples ferrous oxide and ferric oxide make up respectively circa 3 and circa 11%; titanium oxide is present in an amount of slightly over 3% (Washington, 1922). Because of the uniformity of the lavas, a reliable detailed stratigraphy of the Deccan formation is difficult to establish. POORTER Palaeornaynetisch Laboratorium, Fort Hoofddijk, Rijksuniversiteit, Utrecht, The Netherlands Received 3 July 1971 Palaeomagnetic investigations were made on Precambrian rocks from Rogaland (southwestern Norway). Samples from anortho- site masses, a noritic layered intrusion and high grade metamor- phic migmatites, together called the basement, revealed a similar "reversed" magnetization. This is explained by a simultaneous magnetization during uplift after the Sveco-Norwegian regenera- tion. The pole position calculated for the basement rocks i

d 133 ° W. The age that can be assignated to this pole is 850-950×106 y. This is concluded from U/Pb I. Introduction The Rogaland Precambrian consists of high grade metamorphic migmatites enveloping anorthosite mas- ses and a lopolith-shaped noritic intrusion. The whole complex is dissected by dolerite dikes. The determina- tion of the pole-positions belonging to this complex seemed to be useful in establishing a palaeomagnetic stratigraphy for this part of the Baltic Shield, which might in turn enable us to correlate rock formations within this Shield. The Rogaland Precambrian in SW Norway has been the subject of geological and petrographical research of the department of petrography of the Utrecht State University since 1964. This research is directed by TOBI (1965). Previous geological investigations in this area were made by BARTH (1945), MICHOT (1957, 1960), ANTUN (1956), HEIER (1956), and BARTH and DONS (1960). Previous palaeomagnetic research in the Roga- land area has been carried out by STORETVEDT (1965) and STORETVEDT and GIDSKEHAUG (1968) on the Egersund dolerite dikes. 2. Discussion of the results The similar overall magnetic directions of the lopo- lith, the migmatite complex and the anorthosite masses, suggest a simultaneous magnetization. Hence, if the remanence is thermal in origin, a simultaneous cooling of these rock formations has to be assumed. The range of blocking temperatures, determined for the character- istic magnetizations, points to a temperature range of 550 to 650°C. This temperature range fits the tempera- tures involved in the amphibolite and granulite facies metamorphism of the migmatites. It is presumed that the characteristic magnetization originated during the cooling after this metamorphic event. The simultaneous cooling of the lopolith and the anorthosite masses together with the migmatites can be explained by a regional uplift. The variation in the direction of remanent magnetism with altitude has been studied. The palcomagnetic data reveal the occurrence of a reversal of the earth's magnetic field at ar altitude of about 975 meters at Amarkantak as well as the unstable behavior of the geomagnetic field near the polarity transition. These data are at variance with the observation of the same reversal of magnetic field at an altitude of about 625 meters in the palcomagnetic study of several other vertical sequenc'es in the Deccan traps. Gacii (Received 1970 January 22)t Summary Measurements on samples from 20 sites in the Ethiopian flood basalt succession yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 80.8" N, 167-7" E with a circle of confidence of 4.3". Szalay, Director of the Institute for Nuclear Research at Debrecen. A single specimen from each oriented core (sample) is measured and the unit Cretaceous, Tertiary and Quarternary palawmagnetic results 69 The measurement-demagnetization sequence gives a set of at least five directions for each core (independently oriented sample). A consecutive pair of these directions is taken for each core from the unit and the mean direction for the set is found. The procedure is then repeated for all possible combinations of pairs of directions to find which gives the least scatter. The corresponding mean direction is defined as the best direction for the unit. Least scatter is taken to give the largest value of the precision parameter, k = (N- l)/(N-R) (Fisher 1953) since this is readily calculated. (See for instance Irving 1964). With these facts in mind an objective method of choosing the best direction for each core as well for the unit as a whole is needed. When combined with measurements made on rocks from sites some 10 km away from ours, two paths con- necting these transitional virtual poles may be traced, one for the lower Pliocene and the other for the upper Pliocene. Both cross central Russia and the Indian Ocean. Palaeosecular variations of the geomagnetic field have been investigated by restricting our studies to flows which yield virtual poles at latitudes higher than 45" and the dispersion of cleaned R.M. directions obtained from such flows agree with world-wide average values. Thermomagnetic, ore microscope and electron microprobe investigations have been made and the shape of the thermomagnetic curves is related to evidence of both low and high temperature oxidation. 1. Introduction The volcanic rocks of Kyushu Island, Japan range in age from Miocene to Pleistocene (Table 1). Palaeomagnetic studies on them have previously been reported by Kawai er al. (1961, 1962) and also by Nomura (1967). The latter dis- covered some lava flows whose virtual geomagnetic poles computed after A.F. and thermal cleaning of the N.R.M., are situated in low latitudes and suggested that they record geomagnetic field directions during polarit

omagnetic poles lie in S.E. Australia (Figs 6 and 8). At fist we wondered whether an error of 180" had been made in the orientation of samples from these sites (we thought the wrong end of the compass needle might have been read). If this were so, these sites would belong to polarity class N. Creer and Y. ispir* (Received 1969 December 18)t Summary Some of these Cenozoic basalts are magnetized in either the normal or reversed direction of the axial dipole field but some others are magnetized obliquely. The remanences of the latter are quite as stable as the normal or reversed flows and are interpreted as recording geomagnetic field directions during polarity transitions. When combined with measurements made on rocks from sites some 10 km away from ours, two paths con- necting these transitional virtual poles may be traced, one for the lower Pliocene and the other for the upper Pliocene. Conclusion In the light of the variations observed in the Swett ignimbrite it is debatable how accurately these rocks reflect the geomagnetic field direction at the time of their deposition. But the directions of the Needles Range and Leach Canyon ignimbrites are clearly outside the range of any reasonable variations one might expect within a single flow. The possibility of remagnetization at a later time can be rejected since it could result in a direction only closer to the present pole. ‘Anomalous’ poles are fairly commonly observed in Tertiary rocks (e.g. Irving 1964, Gromm6 1965). Mort of these results are based on igneous rocks which cool below their Curie point in a very short time and thercfore represent spot readings. imbrites are in the rhyolite-dacite composition range and are welded to various degrees. The main minerals are quartz, sanidine, plagioclase, hornblende, and biotite but these rarely comprise more than 30 per cent of the rock, the remainder being glass. The lateral lithologic variation within units is usually small whereas the lithologic differences between units are great. The thicknesses range from 10 to about lo00 feet, the average being around 200 feet. The ages used in this paper are those reported by Armstrong (1969). Such a situation is generally met with in the case of igneous activities of uninterrupted nature. In this paper, the palaeomagnetic results on a suite of dolerite dykes, intrusive into Gondwana basins forming a part of the Damodar Valley coaliields of India have been reported, and the inferences based on these results regarding the interrelationship of four different Mesozoic volcanic activities in India are discussed. Geology and palaeomagnetism of the Mesozoic volcanics The Mesozoic volcanic activity in India is represented by four different outcrops of basaltic lavas (Fig. 1). s in fact, that the South Pole made a south-westward discursion during the late Permian towards the coincident Triassic polar regions of South America and Africa. All Permian formations studied so far from South America are reversely magnetized; the inclinations of the magnetic vectors are reversed with respect to the present geomagnetic field inclinations at the sampling sites. The Piaui formation is also reversely magnetized. The magnetizations are believed to date from the Kiaman Magnetic Interval which was first detected and defined from palaeomagnetic studies on Australian Upper Carboniferous and Permian formations (21), (22). A polarity change from ' normal ' to ' reversed ' was demonstrated by Irving (22), in the Upper Carboniferous section of Hunter Valley, New South Wales. Reversed geomagnetic polarity then persisted for almost the whole of the Permian period, the next major polarity change (to ' normal ') occurring in the Lower Triassic. The presence of the Kiaman Magnetic Interval in Permian formations of the U.S.A., the U.S.S.R. and western Europe has been indicated, and the possibility of inter-continental correlation has been discussed by McElhinny (23). Embleton (Received 1970 June 30) Summary Palaeomagnetic data are summarized for two collections of red-beds from the Middle Paganzo formation (Permian age) of La Rioja and San Juan Provinces, north-west Argentina. The thicker succession sampled in La Rioja allows us to trace the movement of the south palaeomagnetic pole which shifted during the Permian from 59.5" S, 2.5" W to 74" S, 52" W. The red-beds from San Juan yield a south palaeomagnetic pole situated at 63" S, 4" W. A basalt which occurs near the base of the La Colina formation (in the Paganzo type area, and directly equivalent to the middle Paganzo) yields a south virtual palaeomagnetic pole at 50" S, 3" E. The results are entirely consistent with previously published palaeomagnetic data for the Permian and Permo-Carboniferous of South America. 1. All Permian formations studied so far from South America are reversely magnetized; the inclinations of the magnetic vectors are reversed with respect to the present geomagnetic field inclinations at the sampling sites. The Piaui formation is also reversely magnetized. The magnetizations are believed to date from the Kiaman Magnetic Interval which was first detected and defined from palaeomagnetic studies on Australian Upper Carboniferous and Permian formations (21), (22). A polarity change from ' normal ' to ' reversed ' was demonstrated by Irving (22), in the Upper Carboniferous section of Hunter Valley, New South Wales. Reversed geomagnetic polarity then persisted for almost the whole of the Permian period, the next major polarity change (to ' normal ') occurring in the Lower Triassic. Embleton (Received 1970 June 30) Summary Palaeomagnetic data are summarized for two collections of red-beds from the Middle Paganzo formation (Permian age) of La Rioja and San Juan Provinces, north-west Argentina. The thicker succession sampled in La Rioja allows us to trace the movement of the south palaeomagnetic pole which shifted during the Permian from 59.5" S, 2.5" W to 74" S, 52" W. The red-beds from San Juan yield a south palaeomagnetic pole situated at 63" S, 4" W. A basalt which occurs near the base of the La Colina formation (in the Paganzo type area, and directly equivalent to the middle Paganzo) yields a south virtual palaeomagnetic pole at 50" S, 3" E. The results are entirely consistent with previously published palaeomagnetic data for the Permian and Permo-Carboniferous of South America. 1. Introduction Palaeomagnetic investigation of South American rock formations commenced in 1956. In 1958, K. M. Creer extended the work to north-west Argentina. of this pole position and its validity for the whole of the Permian period was desirable since the African and Australian palaeomagnetic data have been interpreted (5), (6) such that the palaeomagnetic record of South America appears to be incomplete. In fact, the similarity between the African and Australian data for the Upper Palaeozoic is striking (7), the resulting continental reconstruction supporting that of King's (8) earlier work. y of the Pikes Peak batholith The Pikes Peak batholith is oval shaped in outcrop and follows the axis of a regional north-south anticline formed in the highly metamorphosed Idaho Springs Formation (Fig. 1). On the eastern flanks the granite is overlain by several thousand feet of Upper Cambrian to Cretaceous deposits, many of these in fault contact with the granite (Boos & Boos 1957). Elsewhere it is overlain by sub-horizontal Tertiary sediments and volcanics, associated with Eocene intrusive stocks (Lovering & Goddard 1950). The composition of the batholith varies from older, outermost granodiorite to quartz monzonite to granite in fairly distinct shells (Hutchinson 1960). The texture is massively coarse grained and locally porphyritic. Contact metamorphic effects appear to be rare. Samples were obtained at 1-km intervals westwards along U.S. Highway 24 out of Colorado Springs. Unfortunately the proximity of the Ute Pass Fault may diminish the relevance of such a profile. The fault very roughly parallels the highway, and although it is a high-angle thrust, the granite is locally sheared and brecciated. In the laboratory, several cores 2.5 cm in diameter were drilled from each block sample, and specimens 2.5 cm long were cut from either end of each core. 5. The demagnetization equipment is located in a shielded mu- metal room (residual field < 200 y) and is described by Helsley & Spall (1970). One specimen was demagnetized in successive alternating fields (AF) of 88, 175, 350, 700 and 1400 Oe. There was little vector rotation during this operation. It is typically indicated by observations of a ' minimum intensity * during demagnetization, at which the NRM intensity fluctuates erratically, and the dispersion of directions between-specimens is high. Whatever its origin, the observation of a magnetization whose direction fluctuates greatly, suggests a useful limit to meaningful demagnetization. The second problem arose during thermal demagnetization. Some of the coarse- grained granites could not be heated more than once or twice above 500 "C, because they crumbled. Some of this extra complexity may be due to the exposed character of the sampling sites, most of which were natural outcrops on the tops of ridges. This contrasts with the Arrochar sites all of which were in quarries or streams at low topographic levels. THESIS The radiometric data imply a difference in age of no more than 70 m.y. between the alkali granite and the poststructure basic granophyre (Nicolaysen et al. 1963). If the alkali-granite masses were intruded after the overturning, their primary remanent magnetism should be similar to that of the basic granophyre, assuming restricted polar wander during this short interval. These devia- tions imply, in a general fashion, that large scale relative motions, either rotational or translational, have occurred between Tethys and its northern borderland. But much more data than is presently available is needed before these apparent motions can be evaluated quantitatively, This paper describes new observations (chiefly from Triassic igneous rocks) from the area of the Dolomites which is within the Tethys domain, and is intended as a contribution to this necessary body of knowledge. The Dolomites consist of little disturbed Permian and Mesozoic formations resting on a crystalline basement complex. There is no evidence of regional metamor- phism and nappe tectonics, and if large displacements have occurred they have almost certainly affected the region as a whole. It was for these reasons that this sampling region was chosen. ’ Present address: Laboratorio di Geologia Marina, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, via Zamboni 67, Bologna (Italy). (Canada) (Received April 10, 1970) SUMMARY A paleomagnetic survey of Middle and Upper Triassic porphyrites, dykes, and tuffites from the Dolomites (Eastern Alps, Italy) has yielded an average direction (based on 57 samples from 12 collecting localities) with declination 329OE of true north and inclination +25O after magnetic cleaning and correction for geological dip. The declination deviates from that of %table” Northern Europe by about 50 O, but the inclination agrees well with the expected value. This indicates that the Dolomites area has rotated 50* anticlockwise relative to northern Europe since the Triassic but there is no evidence of relative changes in latitude. These devia- tions imply, in a general fashion, that large scale relative motions, either rotational or translational, have occurred between Tethys and its northern borderland. But much more data than is presently available is needed before these apparent motions can be evaluated quantitatively, This paper describes new observations (chiefly from Triassic igneous rocks) from the area of the Dolomites which is within the Tethys domain, and is intended as a contribution to this necessary body of knowledge. The Dolomites consist of little disturbed Permian and Mesozoic formations resting on a crystalline basement complex. There is no evidence of regional metamor- phism and nappe tectonics, and if large displacements have occurred they have almost certainly affected the region as a whole. It was for these reasons that this sampling region was chosen. ’ Present address: Laboratorio di Geologia Marina, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, via Zamboni 67, Bologna (Italy).
